name: Ivan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the Varley brothers' farm by half six, six hundred outdoor sows in paddocks and eight hundred acres of wheat and barley. First job is the feed round in the old pickup, checking water troughs, fixing any arks the sows have wrecked overnight, then moving electric fence. Neil Varley runs the pigs and Stuart runs the arable, and I go where I'm sent, which is usually the muddiest field.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. Before that I was eighteen years in the army, left as a corporal, and I wanted to work outside with my hands and be home for tea. I'm still learning, I didn't know a gilt from a sow when I started, and Neil has been patient with me. My wife Mira runs the office at the village primary school, and we've got Petra, twelve, and Tomas, eight, and a mortgage on a semi on Station Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can stop going on about it and get back to work. At the Legion I'd say the same. I don't post much online, maybe a thumbs-up on the farm's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays as it is, and that's a good life. The Varleys are fair, the farm is doing well, Mira's job is steady, and we've got about five months put by. A world where AI is mostly hype suits a man who left the army to feed pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd finish my pig husbandry certificate that Neil is paying for. I'd keep putting a bit aside every month like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mira runs the school office. Does even a small change touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. She says there's already software that sends the letters home and does the dinner money, and she likes it. In this picture it saves her time, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any worry at all for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disease, I suppose. African swine fever would finish an outdoor herd. But that's farming, and I knew that when I signed up.

I'd say the same at **the Legion** and maybe like the farm's page online.
think: My life stays as it is, and with **the Varleys** being fair, that's a good life.
Mira's job is steady and we've got about **five months** saved.
do: Finish the **pig husbandry certificate** Neil is paying for.
Keep putting a bit **aside every month**, as we always do.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like a quiet Sunday.

Ex-army, he values **routine** and being home for tea.
His only worry is **swine fever**, a farming risk he accepts.

steps.text: Finish the pig husbandry certificate that Neil Varley is paying for
Keep putting part of each month's wages into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to roll up their sleeves and adapt, like we always have. At the Legion I'd say it's the office jobs that get hit, not ours. I'd probably share something about apprenticeships online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Mira I'm worried about. Letters, dinner money, bookings, answering parents, that's her whole job, and that's exactly what the card says goes first. The pigs are fine for now, but our house runs on two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Mira look at a teaching assistant course, because that's work with children, not screens. I'd put another hundred a month aside in case her hours drop. And I'd learn the farm's new feed app once Neil's tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for her mostly. I'm all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mira's job is office work. How does this picture land for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife's job in the school office is letters, dinner money and phone calls, and this picture says all three go first. She says the head would never let her go. I hope she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, I used it to write my CV when I left the army. I'd use it more if Neil does. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either.

fieldNote: He clearly sees **Mira's office job** in the first wave of thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through worse, and families and communities need to pull together. At the Legion I'd say we look after our own. I wouldn't be asking for handouts, but I'd want apprenticeships for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think we're both out of work by 2031. Mira's office job goes in 2028, and three years later robots can do my pig rounds and fencing better than me, and I'm still learning. The Varleys are decent, but they'd have to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, the caravan holiday, the second car. I'd look at rejoining the army reserves for the extra pay and the training. And I'd lean on my brother, who's got a building firm, for weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Like being told your unit's being disbanded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years to AGI and robots three years later. What happens to you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife's school office job goes in 2028, mine goes in 2031, and the mortgage on Station Road goes on regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Petra and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'll manage, because we always have. Petra would want to know if she can still do her riding. Tomas would ask if robots play football.

I'd want **apprenticeships** for the young ones, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get on with it. At the Legion I'd say look after your own and plan. I'd share stuff about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Mira's office job goes around 2031 and mine about 2034. That's time to get her retrained and me into something more skilled on the farm. I'd still have the mortgage, but not the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the pig certificate, then a farm machinery course over two years. I'd save two hundred a month. And I'd push Petra towards a good apprenticeship when she's sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got orders to follow, if you know what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years' warning. What does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd do the teaching assistant course. My wife Mira says nobody will ever let a robot sit with a six-year-old who's crying in the playground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mira do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And Tomas is too young to plan for. He'd be fine either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people put the work in. At the Legion I'd say no excuses. Online I'd share stuff about the trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have time to become the machinery man on the Varley farm. Mira would be a teaching assistant by then. But I'd still worry for the brothers; they might not keep the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the pig certificate and machinery course slowly. I'd keep saving. And I'd make sure the kids get trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, a bit. Ten years isn't forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to plan. Does that make you feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, but not completely. If the Varleys sell to a big company, I'm out regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd like to be the man who keeps the Varleys' (his bosses') machines running, not the man they replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mira and I would both be out in three years. What would help is apprenticeships and training for adults, paid for by employers, not handouts. A man of forty-three can learn a new trade if somebody gives him the chance and a wage while he does it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How it feels to start over twice. I left the army at forty and started over. I'd do it again, but I'd rather not.
